newsitem.title: THAILAND: New Thai government to curb agencies' spending.
newsitem.headline: New Thai government to curb agencies' spending.

text.p: The Thai government on Monday said it would cut unnecessary spending and surplus funds held by state agencies to stabilise the economy and narrow a wide current account deficit.
Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh said he would review the budget of state agencies with a view to trimming some expenditure. Details would be worked out later with respective agencies.
"I will have to strictly adhere to the policy of monetary discipline, but I will not go into details here," he told a gathering of senior government officials.
Budgets that were already approved for some agencies could be subject to review and any surplus funds not already committed by those agencies might have to be withdrawn, he said.

Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan said that state agencies and enterprises should review project priorities because each year the government was investing more than 700 billion baht ($27.45 billion) in them.

"The current account deficit has shown that we are overspending. Our target is to restore economic stability to the country," said Amnuay, who is also deputy premier. "We have to be cautious not to create more problems of inflation, trade and current account deficits."
The central bank has forecast that Thailand's current account deficit will rise by up to 8.3 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1996, against 8.1 percent of GDP in 1995.
The country's deficit is one of the highest in Asia.
Thailand's economy is also slowing and is set to grow at just over six percent after nearly a decade of about nine percent growth until 1995. Exports are sluggish and investment funds have slowed.
Amnuay also urged government agencies to liberalise their policies, end their monopolies in certain sectors of the economy, eliminate quota systems and promote competitiveness.
The Thai telecommunications sector is an example of a heavily protected business sector.
